{"id": "59:24/q23", "question": "How does the glorification clause work grammatically and rhetorically?", "turns_on": "The notes address different features of the same clause.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q23/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to 'to Him belong the most beautiful names'.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr makes the following al-ʿAzīz clause coordinate with it."}, {"id": "59:24/q23/p2", "position": "The imperfect verb suggests continually renewed praise.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī calls it a reminder to deficient creatures of abiding divine perfection."}, {"id": "59:24/q23/p3", "position": "The placement of 'to Him' restricts glorification exclusively to God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites the preposition and object restriction."}, {"id": "59:24/q23/p4", "position": "One mā covers both heavens and earth, hinting that earth shares heaven's elevation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī reads the joining as a sign of perfection; al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the single mā here with al-Ḥadīd's opening and its subsequent talk of earthly people."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q24", "question": "Is there a variant wording of the glorification clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the reference to the heavens appears in this transmitted reading.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q24/p1", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd reads 'and whatever is in the earth,' omitting heavens.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports this reading."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q25", "question": "What does al-ʿAzīz convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on unconquerable sovereignty generally or its punitive effect.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q25/p1", "position": "God is invincible, overpowering, and unassailable in dominion.", "reasons": "Muqātil stresses dominion; Ibn Kathīr says unassailable; al-Biqāʿī adds no equal, difficult to reach and urgently needed. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls Him the unconquered victor; Elmalılı says He governs all causes."}, {"id": "59:24/q25/p2", "position": "God has power to take severe vengeance on enemies and unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās make retribution explicit; Elmalılı notes Qurʾānic pairings of might and vengeance."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q26", "question": "What does al-Ḥakīm convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the term is read as wise action, rulership, or the sole source of human wisdom.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q26/p1", "position": "God acts, governs, and commands with exact wisdom, free from defect and for creatures' benefit.", "reasons": "Muqātil connects it to command; al-Ṭabarī to wise governance; al-Naḥḥās to flawless acts; Ibn Kathīr to law and decree. Al-Biqāʿī describes firm irreversible judgment and al-Ḥarālī restraining for good, medicine as bodily analogy, and religious striving as another. Elmalılı and Kuran Yolu connect wisdom and proper command. Al-Biqāʿī also connects steadfast governance with the command in 35:6 to treat Satan as an enemy."}, {"id": "59:24/q26/p2", "position": "Al-Ḥakīm can mean al-Ḥākim, the ruler or judge.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports this other sense."}, {"id": "59:24/q26/p3", "position": "True wisdom and judgment belong to God; human wisdom is granted in proportion to knowledge and purification.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites 9:122 for learning rulings, 62:2 for wisdom after purification, and 31:12 for Luqmān. Wisdom eases the burden of obligations; all knowledge is God's."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q27", "question": "Why does the verse end with the Mighty and the Wise?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair's immediate function is to summarize perfection and creation or to close the sūra's wider pattern.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q27/p1", "position": "The two names sum up all divine perfection as power and knowledge, fitting His ordered creation.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı pair perfect power with wise knowledge; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the pair suits the order of creation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the ending assures that the Qurʾān comes from One who cannot be defied and never wastes obedience or reward."}, {"id": "59:24/q27/p2", "position": "The pair recalls the sūra's opening while balancing mercy, judgment, and human choice.", "reasons": "Elmalılı sees it mirroring al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm; Islahi says God could compel worship but wisely tests free human choice."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q28", "question": "How does the verse connect with the surrounding verses and sūra?", "turns_on": "The sources draw different local and whole-sūra links.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q28/p1", "position": "Its ending returns to the sūra's opening glorification, making a ring.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuran Yolu explicitly note the return to 59:1; Islahi links the final attributes to the opening."}, {"id": "59:24/q28/p2", "position": "The creation names follow the preceding divine names to disclose God's acts and prompt gratitude and glorification.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr groups the names in sets matching the sūra's subjects, with local order by analogy or completion; these names address both groups. Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes this verse's creation names from the preceding verses' lordship names. Al-Biqāʿī reads a new proof moving from unseen to manifest."}, {"id": "59:24/q28/p3", "position": "The names complete the mountain example and the call to fear, remembrance, and worship.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī relates the names to the mountain's collapse and prayer through the names; Islahi says they teach fear, love, hope, trust and service after the call to God-consciousness. Kuran Yolu foregrounds mercy and compassion."}, {"id": "59:24/q28/p4", "position": "Universal glorification praises believers and implicitly rebukes unbelievers and hypocrites.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr ties it to the Qurʾān's humbling power and the sūra's legislation about wealth and obedience; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says idols possess none of these attributes. Islahi says hypocrites are especially addressed."}, {"id": "59:24/q28/p5", "position": "The final attributes lead into Sūrat al-Mumtaḥina's test.", "reasons": "Elmalılı links the prospect of being tested before the Mighty and Wise to the next sūra."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q29", "question": "What inward reading is given to the divine names and praise?", "turns_on": "The inward notes focus on manifestation, purification of perception, or human response.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q29/p1", "position": "The names manifest the one Essence's attributes outwardly and inwardly, and creation thereby praises it.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads the creator, maker and shaper as stages of manifestation; al-Tawīlāt al-Najmiyya sees oneness, governance, transcendence, origination, preservation, honor, subjugation and majesty across the names."}, {"id": "59:24/q29/p2", "position": "Divine transcendence excludes associating partners even in vision and thought.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports al-Baqlī's inward gloss."}, {"id": "59:24/q29/p3", "position": "One should conform inner and outward life to the implications of God's attributes.", "reasons": "Islahi makes attributes the basis of religion and sharīʿa; Elmalılı calls for fear, piety, reflection on the verses, and hope in mercy."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q30", "question": "What rewards or healing are reported for reciting al-Ḥashr's ending?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in recitation length, promised reward, and grading.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q30/p1", "position": "Three recitations of refuge and the final three verses morning or evening bring 70,000 angels' prayers and martyrdom if death comes that day or night.", "reasons": "Maʿqil ibn Yasār transmits it. Abū ʿĪsā/al-Tirmidhī calls it gharīb through one route; al-Nashr says ḥasan gharīb, while al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say ḥasan."}, {"id": "59:24/q30/p2", "position": "Reciting the final verses day or night and dying then guarantees Paradise or a martyr's mark.", "reasons": "Abū Umāma reports Paradise without grading; al-Ḥasan says one is stamped among martyrs."}, {"id": "59:24/q30/p3", "position": "Reciting Sūrat al-Ḥashr forgives past and future sins.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bayḍāwī transmit Prophetic reports without a stated grading."}, {"id": "59:24/q30/p4", "position": "The passage from 59:21 to the end cures headache.", "reasons": "Al-Daylamī reports it from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr transmit it."}, {"id": "59:24/q30/p5", "position": "Placing a hand on the head at 59:21 heals every illness except death.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the serial report via Ibn Masʿūd, reciters and Gabriel rare."}, {"id": "59:24/q30/p6", "position": "A verse among the 'Glorifiers' surpasses a thousand verses, possibly 59:24.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports a Prophetic saying and notes an alternative identification as 57:3."}, {"id": "59:24/q30/p7", "position": "The ending has merit in prayer and devotional recitation.", "reasons": "Study Quran calls the passage a Jewel of the Quran and says it is recited in obligatory and voluntary prayers; Elmalılı says reports of its merit are numerous."}]}
{"id": "59:24/q31", "question": "What practical response does this verse and its sūra's ending call for?", "turns_on": "The response varies with the addressed audience.", "positions": [{"id": "59:24/q31/p1", "position": "Reflect on the names, act on the Qurʾān, worship and glorify God with fear, love, trust and hope.", "reasons": "Islahi says believers and hypocrites alike should align beliefs and deeds with the attributes; Elmalılı cites Ibn Masʿūd that action is the Qurʾān's aim, not mere recitation, and connects reflection to 59:18. Kuran Yolu emphasizes mercy in the response."}, {"id": "59:24/q31/p2", "position": "The close strengthens confident believers, resolves weaker ones, and warns hypocrites.", "reasons": "Islahi treats the final names as different appeals to those audiences."}]}

{"id": "62:2/q02", "question": "What does sending the Messenger express here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q02/p1", "position": "God raised and sent a messenger as a favor, guidance, and an expression of His sovereignty and will.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i describes sending from the hidden presence with legal commands and prohibitions; Qatada calls it mercy and guidance; Elmalili likens new knowledge among ignorant Arabs to life from death; Islahi connects God's sovereignty in 62:1 with communicating His directives; Kur'an Yolu says prophethood and revelation depend on God's will."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q03", "question": "Who are the unlettered people named here, and what describes them?", "turns_on": "Whether the label names an ethnic first audience, an absence of scripture, a literacy condition, Meccan origin, or membership in the believing community; al-Tabataba'i and Ibn Atiyya cite context against narrow alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q03/p1", "position": "The Arabs, generally lacking scripture and widespread reading and writing.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Tabari and many later commentators identify the Arabs. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Abbas stress that no book was sent to them; Qatada says there was no scribe, while al-Mufaddal allows that a few wrote. Al-Qurtubi reports Ibn Abbas includes literate Arabs because they were not People of Scripture. Al-Biqa'i says they remained near the natural state of birth. Ibn Kathir cites 3:20; al-Tabataba'i says few could read or write. Islahi identifies them particularly as Ishmaelites and explains that Jews used the designation disparagingly but the Qur'an dignifies it; Study Quran reports al-Tabari's specification of idolatrous Arabs. Kur'an Yolu points to 2:78, 3:20, and 3:75."}, {"id": "62:2/q03/p2", "position": "People unable to write, or unable to read and write, whatever their identity.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda and al-Tabataba'i define the word through literacy; al-Zajjaj and al-Razi describe the original human condition before learning; the Prophet's hadith says this community neither writes nor calculates and counts months by days. Ibrahim's narrower definition permits reading but excludes writing. Al-Qurtubi gives Quraysh as an example of nonwriters; al-Alusi reports a definition limited to inability to write."}, {"id": "62:2/q03/p3", "position": "The people of Mecca or Quraysh specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi's reported view says Quraysh learned writing only late from al-Hira; al-Tabrisi relates the interpretation to Mecca as Mother of Cities. Ibn Atiyya rejects restriction to Quraysh because the verse concerns all Arabs; al-Tabataba'i rejects Meccans as unsuitable to a Medinan sura and its pronoun reference."}, {"id": "62:2/q03/p4", "position": "Anyone without a revealed book, including non-Jews or other peoples outside the scriptural communities.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes the broad reading to al-Razi and cites 3:20; Kur'an Yolu lists the community without its own revealed book. Al-Tabataba'i objects that defining the group as non-Jews or other People of the Book would wrongly constrain the Prophet's mission, citing 3:75."}, {"id": "62:2/q03/p5", "position": "Those who affirm Muhammad and follow his example.", "reasons": "Al-Tustari says affiliation to Muhammad requires emulation and denies membership to one who does not emulate him."}, {"id": "62:2/q03/p6", "position": "Specifically the Ishmaelites who had already accepted faith.", "reasons": "Islahi reads the otherwise general wording by its closing reference to their previous error; he also takes the title to distinguish Ishmaelites."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q04", "question": "What is the derivation of 'ummī'?", "turns_on": "Which noun the adjective is derived from and whether a Meccan derivation would wrongly restrict its scope.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q04/p1", "position": "It relates to one's mother and the original condition at birth, before learned literacy.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya compares a child in the womb; al-Alusi prefers this best-known derivation and includes lack of calculation; Elmalili prefers it in context and adduces the hadith that the community does not write or calculate."}, {"id": "62:2/q04/p2", "position": "It relates to ummah, the community or ordinary human disposition before instruction.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya gives the original human disposition; al-Alusi reports the Arab nation derivation; al-Nasafi derives it from the Arab nation, which did not read or write as other nations did; Elmalili lists this possibility."}, {"id": "62:2/q04/p3", "position": "It relates to Umm al-Qurā, Mecca.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi and Elmalili list this derivation; Ibn Atiyya considers it weak because it would restrict the verse to Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q05", "question": "How did writing spread among the Arabs?", "turns_on": "The reports give different initial locations and populations.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q05/p1", "position": "Writing began for Arabs at al-Ta'if, whose people learned from al-Hira, ultimately from al-Anbar.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj reports the Ta'if to Hira to Anbar chain; al-Nasafi and al-Alusi repeat it, al-Alusi saying Hira's people were from Anbar."}, {"id": "62:2/q05/p2", "position": "Some Quraysh learned writing from al-Hira late in the pre-Islamic age.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi includes this in the report that confines the unlettered to Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q06", "question": "How does the following verse's 'others' attach to the people and teaching named here?", "turns_on": "Whether 'others' is coordinated with the earlier genitive group or with the object of 'teaches'.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q06/p1", "position": "It is genitive, attached to 'the unlettered' with an implied 'among'.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi supplies an understood fī, yielding 'among other unlettered people'."}, {"id": "62:2/q06/p2", "position": "It is accusative, attached to the object pronoun in 'teaches them'.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi says the Prophet thereby teaches other believers who follow his religion."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q07", "question": "How is 'al-ummiyyīn' read?", "turns_on": "Whether omission of the nisba yāʾ is admitted as a variant.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q07/p1", "position": "It is read with the ordinary nisba yāʾ; no disagreement in the sura is reported.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid states that there is no reading disagreement throughout Surat al-Jumu'a."}, {"id": "62:2/q07/p2", "position": "A variant omits the nisba yāʾ, yielding al-amīn or a shortened al-ummiyyīn.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports al-amīn and al-Alusi reports omission of the nisba yāʾ."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q08", "question": "Who is the Messenger, and in what sense is he 'from them'?", "turns_on": "Whether membership expressed by min also conveys the characteristic of unletteredness or only common people and origin.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q08/p1", "position": "He is Muhammad, a human Arab of their own people, lineage, and language.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and al-Tabrisi cite 9:128; al-Razi also cites 23:32. Al-Baghawi says shared language makes the proof compelling. Al-Qurtubi reports kinship across Arab tribes except Taghlib, which Ibn Ishaq excludes from his ancestry on account of Christianity. Al-Wahidi praises his lineage, standing, character, and parents. Islahi says his belonging prevents detractors from attributing Arab guidance to a foreign people."}, {"id": "62:2/q08/p2", "position": "He is from them in the further sense of sharing their unlettered condition.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, al-Biqa'i, Bursevi, and a group reported by al-Alusi stress shared unletteredness. Al-Alusi notes that partitive min alone establishes membership of the group, not necessarily this property; the group prefers the common distinguishing quality."}, {"id": "62:2/q08/p3", "position": "Min is partitive: he belongs to their group, without necessarily proving that he is unlettered.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi explicitly parses min as partitive and says membership by genus need not transfer the group's literacy description to him."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q09", "question": "Why is an unlettered Messenger from these people a sign or blessing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q09/p1", "position": "His unletteredness fulfilled earlier predictions, aided acceptance through resemblance, and excluded learning his revelation from written books; his knowledge proves his mission.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives the three grounds; al-Qurtubi says each proves the miracle. Al-Wahidi, al-Razi, al-Tabrisi, and Ibn al-Jawzi repeat them, with al-Tabrisi adducing accurate history of past nations. Al-Qushayri sees God granting knowledge without study, citing 4:113 and 42:52; Bursevi quotes Isaiah's prediction, al-Kashifi's Persian couplets (last corrupt), and the Burda on learning in an unlettered orphan; al-Alusi cites that poem too. Al-Biqa'i says reform by one of their own is remarkable; al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i add his recitation despite no study. Al-Wahidi describes revelation surpassing Arab eloquence despite their failure to imitate it."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q10", "question": "Does being sent among the unlettered limit his mission to them?", "turns_on": "Whether naming the initial Arab recipients implies exclusivity despite verses explicitly addressing all humanity.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q10/p1", "position": "No; the Arab or Ishmaelite first audience is compatible with a universal mission.", "reasons": "Al-Razi cites 34:28 and says naming a group does not exclude others, comparing 29:48. Ibn Kathir says the favor was emphatic for first recipients and cites 43:44, 26:214, 7:158, 6:19, 11:17. Al-Biqa'i appeals to explicit texts and decisive proofs. Bursevi says a supposed restriction is overridden by the explicit universal statement. Al-Tabataba'i describes an Arabic first phase followed by addresses to Jews, Christians, Magians, and rulers; he says Abraham's prayer in 2:12

Islahi says the Prophet completed the specific Ishmaelite mission while his followers carry the universal mission as witnesses until Judgment."}, {"id": "62:2/q10/p2", "position": "Specifying the unlettered means the Prophet was sent only to the Arabs.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports the People of the Book's inference; he objects that mention of one group is not exclusion of all others. Bursevi expressly refutes the claim."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q11", "question": "Why say 'from them' rather than 'from themselves'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q11/p1", "position": "Minhum suits the wider group of Quraysh and other Arabs, believers and unbelievers; min anfusihim suggests closer intimacy.", "reasons": "Al-Samarra'i contrasts the intimacy and distinction of min anfusihim with simple group membership in minhum, using 3:164; context can still add honor or closeness to minhum."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q12", "question": "How is the Messenger's reciting described grammatically and lexically?", "turns_on": "The notes address both the construction's grammatical role and the manner conveyed by the verb.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q12/p1", "position": "Yatlū alayhim is a circumstantial description of the Messenger, coordinated with the subsequent tasks.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas calls it an accusative circumstantial phrase modifying rasūl; al-Tabataba'i calls the phrase a description, while al-Alusi identifies the coordination of later verbs with it."}, {"id": "62:2/q12/p2", "position": "Tilāwa means sustained, successive recitation, a narrower act than broadly voicing letters.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says one elevated passage follows another repeatedly; Bursevi likens it to study or regular litanies and contrasts wider qirā'a."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q13", "question": "What are the signs he recites, and what does their recitation achieve?", "turns_on": "Whether ayat points chiefly to the Qur'an as recited text or to its functions as proof and legal clarification.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q13/p1", "position": "The signs are the Qur'an, conveying revelation, rulings, proof, and guidance.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and al-Dahhak identify the Qur'an; al-Tabrisi includes lawful and forbidden matters, proofs and rulings. Al-Wahidi says its proofs answer falsehood and dispel doubt and disbelief. Kur'an Yolu stresses conveying revelation as received. Bursevi and al-Biqa'i stress the miracle of an unlettered reciter."}, {"id": "62:2/q13/p2", "position": "They are manifest proofs of his prophethood and the signs distinguishing truth and falsehood or setting out law.", "reasons": "Al-Razi permits both explicit evidence of mission and legal signs; al-Wahidi speaks of proof overcoming falsehood."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q14", "question": "What does the Messenger's purification mean?", "turns_on": "Whether tazkiya names inner and moral cleansing, the call and practices that cause it, or collection of alms.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q14/p1", "position": "He removes idolatry, disbelief, corrupt beliefs, sins, and bad conduct, cultivating faith and virtue.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas specifies pure hearts through faith; Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil specify disbelief and sins; Ibn Atiyya adds growth in good. Al-Razi adds vile speech and deeds; al-Nasafi adds jahiliyya's vices; al-Biqa'i adds base morals and deviant beliefs and his loving gaze. Al-Tabataba'i traces tazkiya to wholesome growth and describes habituated virtue perfecting humanity; Elmalili adds spiritual flourishing and clearer minds. Islahi connects cleansing to divine purity in 62:1; Kur'an Yolu describes spiritual and ethical education."}, {"id": "62:2/q14/p2", "position": "He calls people to obedience and the means of purity, so that following them reforms them.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas says obedience is what renders them purified; al-Razi reports calling to what makes them pious; al-Tabrisi includes such a call alongside cleansing; Ibn Zayd says the Book and righteous deeds are means."}, {"id": "62:2/q14/p3", "position": "He takes their zakat or alms.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi attributes the interpretation to al-Suddi as zakat of their deeds; al-Qurtubi transmits it as taking alms."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q15", "question": "How does purification reach later believers, and who ultimately purifies?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet's traces and his inheritors extend purification and teaching beyond his Companions, in proportion to believers' receptivity.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says longing strengthens adherence to Qur'an and Sunna and deepens practice. Bursevi says perfected inheritors teach later believers the Qur'an's realities after the Prophet taught the Companions directly."}, {"id": "62:2/q15/p2", "position": "God is the true purifier, manifested through the Perfect Human and the Messenger's action.", "reasons": "Bursevi invokes 4:49 and 4:80 to connect divine agency with the Perfect Human as manifestation of divine attributes."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q16", "question": "Why does purification come before teaching in this wording?", "turns_on": "The order of the Prophet's actual education versus the ranking of qualities requested in Abraham's prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q16/p1", "position": "Moral formation precedes true knowledge in educating believers, and each named benefit is a distinct divine favor.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i says ethical formation comes first in the Prophet's education. Al-Biqa'i says its contextual priority counters affection for disbelievers. Al-Irshad, reported by Bursevi, and al-Alusi distinguish recitation's theoretical improvement from purification's practical perfection, even though teaching follows recitation in actual occurrence; the wording displays separate bounties."}, {"id": "62:2/q16/p2", "position": "In Abraham's prayer knowledge comes before purification because knowledge ranks earlier and higher in what is requested.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes the order in 2:129, which requests realization of the qualities, from this verse's description of actual formation."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q17", "question": "What does 'the Book' taught by the Messenger mean?", "turns_on": "Whether kitab denotes revelation as text and rulings, the skill of writing, knowledge gained through it, or law as an institution.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q17/p1", "position": "The Qur'an or revealed scripture, including its wording, commands, prohibitions, explanation, and admonition.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari describes divine commands, prohibitions and ordinances; Muqatil includes lawful and unlawful admonition. Al-Tabataba'i calls teaching explanation of verse wording and difficult passages. Al-Biqa'i describes revelation containing religious and worldly good. Ibn Ishaq, as reported by al-Mawardi, treats knowledge of good and evil through the Book as leading to action. Bursevi says it can include the wording, and Elmalili includes Qur'anic instruction. Al-Alusi and al-Tabataba'i say repeating 'signs' and 'Book' marks distinct blessings."}, {"id": "62:2/q17/p2", "position": "Writing with a pen and literacy taught to the Arabs.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says writing spread through religion's command to record matters; al-Qurtubi, al-Mawardi and Bursevi transmit him; Elmalili includes literacy in teaching."}, {"id": "62:2/q17/p3", "position": "Knowledge of good and evil, directing people to do one and avoid the other.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi and Bursevi attribute this interpretation to Muhammad ibn Ishaq."}, {"id": "62:2/q17/p4", "position": "Divine law or sharīʿa, whose implementation requires authority.", "reasons": "Islahi identifies al-kitab as law and connects enforcement with power and authority; Elmalili includes the rulings to be applied."}]}

{"id": "62:2/q19", "question": "What does teaching the Book and wisdom accomplish and whom can it reach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q19/p1", "position": "It forms the first and later believers in revelation and practice and is itself a sign of the Prophet's mission.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd extends teaching to later generations until the Hour, citing 9:100 and 59:10, and contrasts many foremost early people with fewer later ones via 56:11, 56:13, 56:27, 56:39. {"id": "62:2/q20", "question": "How should the repeated titles 'signs', 'Book', and 'wisdom' be understood?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q20/p1", "position": "Each title brings out a distinct benefit of the same revelation and so marks a separate blessing.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi makes this explicit; al-Tabataba'i reports the proposal for signs and Book. {"id": "62:2/q21", "question": "What is the force and syntax of 'wa-in kānū ... la-fī'?", "turns_on": "The notes supply complementary particle parsing and clause placement.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q21/p1", "position": "In is a lightened emphatic inna; the lām marks the affirmative predicate and distinguishes it from negative or conditional in.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi calls the separating lām necessary; al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi identify the lighter particle; Bursevi excludes both conditional and negative readings; al-Alusi distinguishes conditional in; Ibn Ashur adds that the lightened particle governs neither noun nor predicate and kāna fills its expected place; al-Tabataba'i concurs."}, {"id": "62:2/q21/p2", "position": "The clause is parenthetical within the Messenger's enumerated tasks.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur places the parenthesis either between coordinated elements or between the pronouns and the comitative object."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q22", "question": "What does their former manifest error consist of?", "turns_on": "Whether manifest error is specified as idolatry and jahiliyya or expressed more generally as distance from truth.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q22/p1", "position": "Before the Prophet's mission they were plainly astray through idolatry, unbelief, ignorance, and corrupt conduct.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Dahhak, Bursevi and others specify polytheism and idols. Al-Qurtubi says 'before' means before the Messenger or his sending. Al-Tabrisi calls it departure from truth and religion; al-Biqa'i says they abandoned Ishmael's religion and cites scorn for seekers like Zayd ibn Amr. Al-Nasafi says no error was greater; Elmalili adds bewilderment. Ibn Kathir says most people, not only Arabs, had strayed: Arabs altered Abraham's religion, scriptural communities altered their books, with a tiny remnant following Jesus. Al-Tabataba'i sees the clause as praise of divine favor after glorification."}, {"id": "62:2/q22/p2", "position": "They were far from truth in a broad sense, a state needing the Messenger's guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives the general expression; al-Tabrisi names departure from truth and religion. Islahi recalls long ignorance as a contrast with later honor."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q23", "question": "Does the description of former error include every Arab without exception?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance in monotheism removes the named individuals from a judgment that may also concern revealed law.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q23/p1", "position": "It describes the people predominantly; a few monotheists were exceptions.", "reasons": "Sa'di al-Mufti names Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Zayd ibn Amr, and Quss ibn Sa'ida and reports the Prophet's saying each would rise as a community alone; al-Alusi likewise names Waraqa."}, {"id": "62:2/q23/p2", "position": "Even monotheist exceptions remained astray regarding revealed laws and rulings, so the description applies in that respect.", "reasons": "Bursevi accepts their guidance in divine oneness but rejects Sa'di's exemption as to law; he also says 93:7 does not mean the Prophet committed idolatry or sins."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q24", "question": "Why mention their prior error and emphasize it here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q24/p1", "position": "It magnifies the divine favor and need for guidance, and rebuts the idea that such people taught the Prophet his revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya makes the before-and-after contrast; al-Baydawi and Bursevi link it to need and the absence of a human teacher. Al-Biqa'i says the emphasis answers those who thought they followed sound religion and warns of later straying; the visible error heightens the miracle and urgency. Al-Alusi says it dispels a human-instruction hypothesis, and Islahi urges gratitude for ascent from long ignorance and dishonor."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q25", "question": "How does this verse fulfill Abraham's prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q25/p1", "position": "Muhammad's mission among Ishmael's descendants answers Abraham's prayer for a messenger who recites, teaches, and purifies.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites 2:129 and places the sending after a long prophetic break; al-Tabataba'i says Abraham and Ishmael's prayer embraces Ishmaelite descendants beyond Mecca. Islahi identifies the same tasks, sees Muhammad as fulfilling Abraham's prayer and Jesus' prediction, and refers to the discussion of the Prophet's attributes in al-Baqara. Ibn al-Jawzi points to 2:129 for the preceding teaching; Kur'an Yolu also compares 2:129, 2:151, and 3:164; Study Quran lists those recurrent task verses and relates the teaching to 3:81, 4:54, 5:110, and 4:113."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q26", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding sūras and opening glorification?", "turns_on": "The notes trace distinct links to the opening divine names, the previous sūra, and the rest of al-Jumu'a.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q26/p1", "position": "The praise of the Messenger follows the opening account of God's attributes and turns the passage from divine oneness to prophethood and favor.", "reasons": "Al-Razi notes the turn after 62:1; al-Tabataba'i says glorification grounds the mission's power to guide and perfect, and that the first three verses frame divine favor. Islahi says the Messenger manifests the Sovereign's directives and divine purity; al-Samarra'i notes that the tasbih opening is followed by sending the Messenger."}, {"id": "62:2/q26/p2", "position": "It answers the previous sūra's account of Jesus and his followers by recalling prediction of Muhammad and Abraham's prayer for the Ishmaelites.", "reasons": "Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, reported by al-Biqa'i, says praise of this community counters a possible impression from 61:14 that Jesus' followers are superior; Islahi identifies Jesus' prediction and Abraham's prayer and says the Ishmaelites must value this favor despite Jewish opposition."}, {"id": "62:2/q26/p3", "position": "The sūra repeatedly centers the human recipients of the Messenger's mission and those who come later.", "reasons": "Al-Samarra'i says this is why al-Jumu'a repeats mā. Islahi says the whole sura stresses the favor to Arabia's unlettered people, whom Jews envy; a later incident and the Muslims' weaknesses showed that many undervalued it."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q27", "question": "What response does the favor of this mission call for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q27/p1", "position": "Recipients should recognize, honor, and preserve God's favor of guidance and carry it to others.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says the verse enumerates favors to the Arabs; Islahi says Ishmaelites should resist Jewish schemes, honor the favor, encourage others, and serve as vanguard witnesses to humanity. Kur'an Yolu says revelation and prophethood are bestowed by divine will. Al-Biqa'i reads purification of stubborn people as evidence of divine power, contrasting Israelite refusal and showing power to purify all rational beings."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q28", "question": "Which specific conversions illustrate the Messenger's purification and guidance?", "turns_on": "Different narrated cases of guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q28/p1", "position": "Umayr ibn Wahb converted after plotting with Safwan to kill the Prophet, then brought the fleeing Safwan back after Mecca's conquest; Safwan converted too.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i recounts the plot after Badr, the Prophet's guidance of Umayr, and Umayr's later standing as a leading Companion."}, {"id": "62:2/q28/p2", "position": "Al-Tufayl ibn Amir al-Dawsi received a luminous sign, then called his family and people, all of whom accepted Islam.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i relates the light, the call, and the response."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q29", "question": "What understanding of wisdom and error follows from the Qur'an's transformation of human outlook?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q29/p1", "position": "Revelation corrects materialist assumptions about life and causation, teaches true beliefs and virtuous action through i

{"id": "62:2/q30", "question": "Is close study of Qur'anic meanings a forbidden kind of interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether teaching the Book and wisdom includes inquiry into Qur'anic meanings.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q30/p1", "position": "No; prophetic teaching of the Qur'an's meanings warrants study beyond bare recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i rejects the assertion that exegesis is merely recitation and close study is prohibited."}, {"id": "62:2/q30/p2", "position": "Exegesis is only recitation and close study of meaning is forbidden interpretation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports and rejects this claim."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q31", "question": "What inward effect can the appearance of God's beauty or majesty have on a servant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q31/p1", "position": "Beauty gathers thoughts around divine generosity; majesty consumes the self in God and effaces concern for this world and the next.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri distinguishes the heart's response to beauty from the secret heart's response to majesty."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q32", "question": "What divine qualities underlie the Messenger's commission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q32/p1", "position": "God knows and governs all things without doubt, bodily organs, tools, reflection, or consultation.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites 6:59 for knowledge of seen, unseen, public and secret things; he says God knows without thinking, sees without eyes, creates without tools, speaks without tongue or sound, wills without resolve, and decrees without counsel."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q33", "question": "What ancillary textual or scholarly notes accompany discussion of this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q33/p1", "position": "Some commentators direct the reader to parallel explanations of the same prophetic tasks and expressions elsewhere.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi points to his earlier al-Baqara treatment; Abu Hayyan points to 3:164; Ibn al-Jawzi points to 2:78 for the unlettered and 2:129 for teaching; Islahi points to his al-Baqara account against Hadith rejecters; Kur'an Yolu points to 7:157-158 for the unlettered Prophet and 2:269 for wisdom."}, {"id": "62:2/q33/p2", "position": "Al-Wahidi composed his commentary to address meanings, parsing, obscure points, and variant readings at scholars' urging amid neglect of learning.", "reasons": "He says a few genuine scholars remain virtuous and learning remains honorable despite fashionable pretense and neglect."}]}
{"id": "62:2/q34", "question": "What minor phonetic and poetic reading matters are reported?", "turns_on": "Different phonetic or metrical issues in the source notes.", "positions": [{"id": "62:2/q34/p1", "position": "Assimilation of two lām letters is permitted.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas allows the assimilation."}, {"id": "62:2/q34/p2", "position": "A reading with a still mīm is defensible on accurate transmission and poetic meter.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni defends Sibawayh's hearing and says Abu al-Abbas's alternative cannot fit the cited meter."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q01", "question": "When is 'that Day' of presentation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q01/p1", "position": "It is the Day of Resurrection and judgment, broad enough to include the trumpet blasts, swoon, resurrection, reckoning, and final destinations.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī names Resurrection. {"id": "69:18/q02", "question": "How does 'that Day you are presented' connect grammatically to the preceding trumpet clause?", "turns_on": "Which clause answers the earlier conditional and whether this time clause is new or a substitution.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q02/p1", "position": "The presentation clause answers the preceding conditional about the trumpet.", "reasons": "The Shaykh says tuʿraḍūn answers idhā in fa-idhā nufikha. {"id": "69:18/q03", "question": "Why is 'that Day' repeated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q03/p1", "position": "Its repetition magnifies the terror of the Day.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr counts five mentions of the day overall: the first echoes idhā in the trumpet clause and four follow it; the events begin with the trumpet blast."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q04", "question": "Who is addressed by 'you will be presented'?", "turns_on": "Whether the universal address is described as all creation or specifically those accountable.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q04/p1", "position": "All people or all creation are addressed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the address encompasses all creation; Ibn ʿĀshūr points to context and following details. {"id": "69:18/q05", "question": "What does being presented mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q05/p1", "position": "People are brought before God for reckoning, questioning, judgment, and recompense.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, and others state presentation before the Lord. Al-Qushayrī adds rebuke or punishment as due; Tustarī adds that everything was already recorded in God's prior knowledge. Al-Qurṭubī cites 18:48. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, and Elmalılı liken it to a ruler inspecting troops; Biqāʿī adds selection of the good for honor and the corrupt for punishment. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the lexical sense of showing goods to a buyer or troops to a commander, allows a literal display, and says presentation alludes to reckoning. Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses the seller/buyer likeness and cites 18:48. Study Quran cites 11:18 for 'brought forth.' Al-Iṣlāḥī says no place or object remains to hide someone after the heavens and earth are destroyed. Ibn Kathīr stresses God's knowledge of inner and outer states."}, {"id": "69:18/q05/p2", "position": "The presentation includes people's inward forms of their deeds and actions.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī explicitly specifies these inward forms."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q06", "question": "Why are people presented when God already knows them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q06/p1", "position": "The display reveals people's condition, establishes proof, and makes divine justice visible; it does not give God new knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says God knows deeds by His essence and exposes them for creation to see. Al-Qurṭubī denies that presentation informs God and cites 18:48. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say it manifests justice; the latter adds proof and God's prior knowledge. Bursawī compares 82:9. Elmalılı contrasts this complete disclosure with worldly reviews and cites 14:48. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God's dominion and knowledge are always true but become unmistakable on that Day."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q07", "question": "How many presentations occur, and what happens at each?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q07/p1", "position": "There are three: two for disputes, excuses, argument or accounting, then records fly into people's hands, right or left.", "reasons": "Qatāda transmits this, sometimes tentatively or as a mursal report. {"id": "69:18/q09", "question": "How exacting can a person's questioning be?", "turns_on": "The examples differ in subject and reported duration; the notes do not argue one against the other.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q09/p1", "position": "God asks even about favors and the time and gatherings devoted to Him.", "reasons": "Tustarī gives recognition of granted hours and gatherings and an answered request for a wife as examples, then asks how much more severe questioning about disobedience will be."}, {"id": "69:18/q09/p2", "position": "A believer may be held before God for a single sin for a hundred years.", "reasons": "Tustarī reports this statement from ʿUtba the ascetic."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q10", "question": "How should one prepare for the great presentation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q10/p1", "position": "Audit and amend oneself, weigh one's deeds before judgment, and persistently seek God over past failings.", "reasons": "ʿUmar urges self-accounting and weighing oneself before the final account. {"id": "69:18/q12", "question": "Why is 'you are presented' passive?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q12/p1", "position": "The presentation itself is terrifying, and the statement comes from the Almighty.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī gives both grounds for the passive wording."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q13", "question": "How should the Throne imagery associated with the presentation be understood?", "turns_on": "Whether presentation and Throne language requires bodily presence or is figurative or left uninterpreted.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q13/p1", "position": "Presentation and the bearing of the Throne imply that God is on the Throne and carried with it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports the anthropomorphists arguing that bearing the Throne would otherwise be pointless. Bursawī reports their claim that God is carried and present there."}, {"id": "69:18/q13/p2", "position": "The scene uses familiar royal imagery to show divine majesty, judgment, dominion, or power without bodily location or need.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī's people of divine oneness argue literal sitting would make God dependent on angels and imply their greater power; they compare God's house, the stone called His right hand, and record-keeping angels, none of which imply human limitations. He says the Throne, attendants, and assembly follow the custom of kings judging officials. Bursawī interprets coming amid clouds as the coming of God's command and decree; he reads a transformation report as manifestation in an attribute-rank and the vision of a beardless youth as dreamlike, because God lacks bodily qualities. Kur'an Yolu reports theologians reading the Throne as dominion and its bearers as angels administering the universe, with divine rule continuing after the material world's collapse; it also reports Ibn ʿĀshūr and Asad taking its bearing as decisive manifestation of power, citing 40:7."}, {"id": "69:18/q13/p3", "position": "Accept the wording of these ambiguous verses while leaving their meaning unknown.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu attributes this to Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Ashʿarī, and al-Māturīdī."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q14", "question": "What does 'ʿarsh' in the preceding scene refer back to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q14/p1", "position": "Its earlier Qurʾanic discussion, especially al-Aʿrāf 7:54.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu points to that earlier discussion without adding a new definition here."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q15", "question": "Who are the eight bearers of the Throne in the preceding scene?", "turns_on": "The Qurʾan does not explain who the eight are; the alternatives are contextual inferences.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q15/p1", "position": "Eight angels or Throne-bearers.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says the Qurʾan does not identify them and commentators infer this from context; its translation favors angels."}, {"id": "69:18/q15/p2", "position": "Eight persons.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this alternative and says al-Rāzī prefers it."}, {"id": "69:18/q15/p3", "position": "Eight ranks.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this alternative without further grounds."}, {"id": "69:18/q15/p4", "position": "Eighty angels.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this alternative without further grounds."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q16", "question": "How is the trumpet scene before the presentation described?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q16/p1", "position": "A horn-shaped trumpet is blown twice by Isrāfī: the first blast kills the living, and the second raises them.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu gives this as traditional belief and cites 6:73; the scene leads to the presentation after the destruction of the present heavens and earth."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q17", "question": "How is this presentation linked to the surrounding verses and sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q17/p1", "position": "The catastrophe gives way to universal presentation and then the distinct outcomes of the righteous and wicked.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī moves from warning about the Day of Calling to the general scene, then the particular division. Kur'an Yolu says 13–18 explain 1–3 and describe Resurrection and the end of worldly life, citing 18:47."}]}
{"id": "69:18/q18", "question": "Which verb reading occurs in 'lā takhfā'?", "turns_on": "Agreement with a grammatically feminine but nonnaturally feminine and separated subject, plus differing reader attributions.", "positions": [{"id": "69:18/q18/p1", "position": "The verb is feminine, lā takhfā, agreeing with khāfiyah.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ calls both readings sound. The general or majority reading is feminine; Abū Ḥātim prefers it because the subject is feminine. Al-Samīn calls overt feminine marking the default. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that khāfiyah is separated from the verb and not naturally feminine. Reports vary in assigning the masculine reading: al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī say Kufans except ʿĀṣim, while Jishumī includes ʿĀṣim."}, {"id": "69:18/q18/p2", "position": "The verb is masculine, lā yakhfā.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ attributes it to Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and considers both forms sound, comparing paired feminine and masculine verbs for 'the cry seized.' Al-Naḥḥās says a nonliteral feminine subject can take masculine agreement when separated. Abū ʿUbayd prefers yāʾ because it can serve masculine or feminine while tāʾ only feminine, and minkum intervenes. Al-Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite nonnatural femininity and separation.
